title: What is the "this escape" problem during object construction? How does a listener registration or thread start leak a partially constructed object, and how do you fix it with a static factory method or post-construction initialization?

s1_definition.profdef: The "this escape" problem occurs when a reference to an object becomes visible to another thread before the object's constructor has finished. Common causes are registering `this` as a listener inside the constructor, starting a thread from the constructor, or passing `this` to external code during construction. Another thread may then observe the object with uninitialized or partially initialized fields, including final fields that are not yet safely published, leading to subtle bugs. The fix is to never let `this` escape during construction: use a private constructor plus a static factory method, or do the risky registration in a separate initialization step after the object is fully built.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a new bank account is being opened for Rajesh. The clerk is still filling in the balance and account number on the form. Before finishing, the clerk hands a photocopy of the half-filled form to the auditing department. The auditor reads it and sees a blank balance and no account number, then makes a wrong decision. The account object escaped before it was fully built. The right process is: finish the entire form, then hand out copies.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never let `this` leave the constructor — publish the object only after it is fully built, using a static factory or a separate init step.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The "this escape" problem occurs when a reference to an object becomes visible to another thread before the object's constructor has finished. Common causes are registering `this` as a listener inside the constructor, starting a thread from the constructor, or passing `this` to external code during construction. Another thread may then observe the object with uninitialized or partially initialized fields, including final fields that are not yet safely published, leading to subtle bugs. The fix is to never let `this` escape during construction: use a private constructor plus a static factory method, or do the risky registration in a separate initialization step after the object is fully built.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a new bank account is being opened for Rajesh. The clerk is still filling in the balance and account number on the form. Before finishing, the clerk hands a photocopy of the half-filled form to the auditing department. The auditor reads it and sees a blank balance and no account number, then makes a wrong decision. The account object escaped before it was fully built. The right process is: finish the entire form, then hand out copies.

**One line to remember:** Never let `this` leave the constructor — publish the object only after it is fully built, using a static factory or a separate init step.

sections.s2_technical:
The classic escape is registering as a listener inside the constructor. If you write `source.registerListener(this)` in a constructor, another thread firing events can call back into your object before the constructor returns. At that moment your fields may still hold default values like null or zero. Even final fields are not guaranteed to be visible to other threads until the constructor completes, so the callback can see a broken object.

Starting a thread in a constructor is the same mistake. If you write `new Thread(this).start()` in the constructor, the new thread can run before the object finishes building. The started thread sees half-initialized state. Even just creating an inner class instance that captures `this` and handing it to external code can leak the enclosing object.

The cleanest fix is the static factory method pattern. You make the constructor private so nobody can partially build the object, do all field assignment inside the constructor, and then in a static factory method perform any registration or thread start after the object is fully constructed. For example, `public static SettlementMonitor create(EventSource src) { SettlementMonitor m = new SettlementMonitor(); src.registerListener(m.listener); return m; }` registers only after the object exists completely.

A second fix is a separate `start()` or post-construction method. In Spring, the `@PostConstruct` annotation marks a method that runs after the bean is fully constructed and dependencies are injected, which is the safe place to register listeners or start background work. Outside Spring you expose an explicit `init()` or `start()` method the caller invokes after construction.

A senior-level nuance is that this is not only a visibility problem but also an ordering one. The Java Memory Model only guarantees that correctly constructed, safely published objects have their final fields visible. Leaking `this` breaks safe publication, so other threads may legally see stale or default values. The rule is simple and absolute: do not publish `this` until the constructor has returned.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India built a settlement monitor that listens for trade-settled events. The first version registered itself as a listener inside its own constructor. Under load, an event fired on another thread the instant the object was created, and the callback ran before the constructor had set the `bankName` and `threshold` fields. The callback saw null and zero, threw a NullPointerException, and dropped a settlement event. This is exactly the this escape problem — the object escaped to the event source before it was fully built.

Problem 2 — The team needed a safe way to build the monitor and only then wire it to the event stream. This is exactly what a static factory method fixes — build fully in a private constructor, then register after construction completes.

The project is a trade settlement monitor. The broken `LeakyMonitor` registers `this` in its constructor to show the bug. The fixed `SafeSettlementMonitor` uses a private constructor and a static `create` factory that registers only after the object exists. An `EventSource` fires settlement events. The demo shows the leaky version seeing uninitialized fields and the safe version working correctly.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an EventSource, a SafeSettlementMonitor created via factory, and two settlement events (2,500,000 and 50,000). The threshold for a "big" trade is 1,000,000.

Step 1 — `SafeSettlementMonitor.create` calls the private constructor. All three fields (`bankName`, `threshold`, `listener`) are assigned before the constructor returns. At this point the object is fully built and nobody outside has a reference.

Step 2 — The factory now calls `source.registerListener(monitor.listener)`. The reference is published only after construction finished, so safe publication holds.

Step 3 — `source.fire("TRD-001", 2500000)` invokes the listener. The `threshold` field is correctly 1,000,000, so the comparison returns true and the event is logged as big.

Step 4 — `source.fire("TRD-002", 50000)` invokes the listener again. The comparison returns false, logged as not big.

Step 5 — There is never a window where the callback sees null `bankName` or zero `threshold`, because the listener was registered after the object was fully constructed.

Final output:

```
INFO: [National Bank of India] trade TRD-001 amount 2500000 big=true
INFO: [National Bank of India] trade TRD-002 amount 50000 big=false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  BROKEN (LeakyMonitor):
    new LeakyMonitor(source)
      │ step 1: source.registerListener(this)   ← this ESCAPES here
      │                                           │
      │                              (another thread fires)
      │                                           ▼
      │                              onSettled() sees bankName=null,
      │                              threshold=0  → NullPointerException
      │ step 2: this.bankName  = "..."   (too late)
      │ step 3: this.threshold = 1000000 (too late)
      ▼

  FIXED (SafeSettlementMonitor.create):
    monitor = new SafeSettlementMonitor()
      │ bankName  = "National Bank of India"
      │ threshold = 1000000
      │ listener  = this::handle
      ▼  (object FULLY built, still private)
    source.registerListener(monitor.listener)   ← safe publication
      │
      ▼
    fire("TRD-001", 2500000) → handle() → threshold correct → big=true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The this escape problem happens when a reference to an object becomes visible to other code, and especially to other threads, before the constructor has finished running. The most common way it sneaks in is registering the object as a listener inside its own constructor, starting a thread from the constructor, or passing this to external code during construction. The danger is that another thread can then call back into the object while its fields are still at their default values, so it sees null references and zero numbers, and even final fields are not guaranteed to be visible until the constructor completes.

The reason this is dangerous and not just theoretical is that the Java Memory Model only promises safe publication for objects that are fully and correctly constructed. If I leak this early, I have broken that promise, and another thread is legally allowed to see stale or default state. In a bank that can mean dropping a settlement event or making a decision on a half-built object, which is unacceptable.

The fix I use is to never let this escape the constructor. The cleanest pattern is a private constructor combined with a static factory method. I assign every field inside the private constructor so the object is complete, and only then, inside the factory method, do I register it as a listener or start any background work. In Spring the equivalent is the PostConstruct annotation, which runs after the bean is fully constructed and dependencies are injected, so that is the safe place to wire up listeners rather than the constructor.

At National Bank of India we hit this exactly in a trade settlement monitor whose first version registered itself as a listener inside its constructor. Under load an event fired on another thread before the constructor had set the bank name and threshold fields, and the callback threw a NullPointerException and dropped the event. We rewrote it with a private constructor and a static create factory that builds the object fully and only then registers it to the event source, and the race disappeared. The sentence I give interviewers is that you must never publish this during construction, because other threads can observe a partially initialized object, and the safe approach is a private constructor with a static factory or a post-construction initialization step that registers the object only after it is fully built.

---

keyPoints: Publishing this during construction — object not fully built
Fix: factory method — construct then publish
